### 11.2 Metaheuristics

A **metaheuristic** is a general strategy that guides simpler heuristics (construction and local search) beyond the first local optimum. Every metaheuristic balances two forces. **Intensification** searches thoroughly near good solutions, and **diversification** moves the search to unexplored regions. **Trajectory methods** (simulated annealing, tabu search, GRASP, large neighborhood search) improve one solution at a time. **Population methods** (genetic algorithms, ant colonies, particle swarms) evolve many solutions together. All the TSP examples use the running instance of Section 11.1, so their gaps can be compared directly.

| Method | Escapes local optima by | Memory | Typical strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simulated annealing | accepting some worse moves at random | none | simple, any neighborhood |
| Tabu search | taking the best non-tabu move, even uphill | tabu list, long-term statistics | scheduling, routing, coloring |
| Genetic algorithm | recombining solutions | population | black-box objectives, many objectives |
| Ant colony | sampling from a learned model | pheromone matrix | constructive problems, dynamic data |
| Particle swarm | particles attracted by good points | personal and swarm bests | continuous nonconvex problems |
| GRASP | randomized greedy restarts | none (or an elite pool) | easy parallelism |
| Large neighborhood search | destroying and rebuilding large parts | operator weights (ALNS) | routing and scheduling with side constraints |

#### Simulated Annealing

**Why it matters.** Simulated annealing (SA) is probably the easiest way to turn hill climbing into a method that escapes local optima. It needs only a neighborhood, a way to evaluate moves, and a temperature schedule. Since its introduction by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi (1983) and Černý (1985), it has been used for chip placement, timetabling, scheduling and many problems where better-tailored methods were not worth building.

**Theory.** In metallurgy, annealing heats a metal and cools it slowly, so the atoms settle into a low-energy crystal structure. Quenching (fast cooling) freezes defects instead. SA mimics this. At each step it picks a **random** neighbor $y$ of the current solution $x$ and computes $\Delta = f(y) - f(x)$. It then applies the **Metropolis rule**:

$$
P(\text{accept } y) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \Delta \le 0, \\ e^{-\Delta / T} & \text{if } \Delta > 0. \end{cases}
$$

At high temperature $T$, almost every move is accepted and the search wanders freely. As $T$ falls, uphill moves become rare, and at $T \to 0$ SA becomes randomized hill climbing. Small uphill steps are accepted much more often than large ones:

| $\Delta$ | $T = 41$ | $T = 5$ | $T = 1$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.976 | 0.819 | 0.368 |
| 10 | 0.784 | 0.135 | 0.00005 |

**Why it works.** At a fixed temperature, SA is a Markov chain (Section 9.2) whose stationary distribution is the Boltzmann distribution $\pi_T(x) \propto e^{-f(x)/T}$. As $T \to 0$, this distribution concentrates on the global optima. Hajek (1988) proved that a logarithmic schedule $T_k = c / \log(1 + k)$, with $c$ at least the depth of the deepest non-global local minimum, reaches a global optimum with probability 1. That schedule is far too slow for practice, so SA in practice is a heuristic.

**Practical schedule.**

- **Initial temperature.** Choose $T_0$ so that a given share of uphill moves is accepted at the start, for example 50%: $T_0 = -\bar{\Delta}^+ / \ln 0.5$, where $\bar{\Delta}^+$ is the mean of sampled uphill deltas.
- **Cooling.** The most common schedule is **geometric cooling** $T \leftarrow \alpha T$ with $\alpha \in [0.8, 0.99]$ and $L$ moves per temperature, often proportional to the neighborhood size.
- **Stopping.** Stop when the acceptance rate has been near zero for a while, or when the time budget ends. Always return the best solution seen, not the last one.
- **Variants.** Reheating after stagnation, adaptive schedules that keep a target acceptance rate, and simpler threshold rules (accept if $\Delta < $ threshold, or "record-to-record travel").

**Example: SA with 2-opt moves.** The trace shows one run. The comparison then varies the cooling rate with 2,000 moves per temperature, from the same random start and over 5 seeds.

```python
import numpy as np

# Reuses D, n, OPT and length() from the Nearest Neighbor and Insertion topic.

def simulated_annealing(t, alpha, steps_per_T, seed, verbose=False):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = list(t); cur = length(t); best, best_t = cur, t[:]

    def random_move():                              # random 2-opt move: edges i and j, i < j
        i, j = sorted(r.choice(n, size=2, replace=False))
        a, b, c, d = t[i], t[i + 1], t[j], t[(j + 1) % n]
        return i, j, D[a, c] + D[b, d] - D[a, b] - D[c, d]

    # Initial temperature: accept an average uphill move with probability 0.5
    ups = [dl for dl in (random_move()[2] for _ in range(1000)) if dl > 0]
    T = -np.mean(ups) / np.log(0.5)
    stage, moves = 0, 0
    while T > 0.1:                                  # frozen: almost no uphill move is accepted
        accepted = 0
        moves += steps_per_T
        for _ in range(steps_per_T):
            i, j, delta = random_move()
            if j - i < 2 or (i == 0 and j == n - 1): continue      # degenerate move
            if delta < 0 or r.random() < np.exp(-delta / T):       # Metropolis rule
                t[i + 1:j + 1] = t[i + 1:j + 1][::-1]
                cur += delta; accepted += 1
                if cur < best - 1e-9: best, best_t = cur, t[:]
        if verbose and stage % 12 == 0:
            print(f"  T = {T:7.2f}  accepted {accepted / steps_per_T:5.1%}  "
                  f"current gap {cur / OPT - 1:6.1%}  best gap {best / OPT - 1:6.1%}")
        T *= alpha                                  # geometric cooling
        stage += 1
    return best_t, moves

r0 = np.random.default_rng(0)
start = list(r0.permutation(n))
print("trace of one run (alpha = 0.95, 2,000 moves per temperature):")
simulated_annealing(start, 0.95, 2000, seed=0, verbose=True)
for alpha, steps in [(0.80, 2000), (0.95, 2000), (0.99, 2000)]:
    runs = [simulated_annealing(start, alpha, steps, seed=s) for s in range(5)]
    gaps = [length(t) / OPT - 1 for t, _ in runs]
    print(f"alpha = {alpha:.2f}: {runs[0][1]:9,d} moves per run, mean gap {np.mean(gaps):5.1%}, "
          f"best {min(gaps):5.1%}")
# trace of one run (alpha = 0.95, 2,000 moves per temperature):
#   T =   41.00  accepted 60.8%  current gap 365.8%  best gap 285.1%
#   T =   22.15  accepted 38.3%  current gap 221.0%  best gap 205.6%
#   T =   11.97  accepted 18.9%  current gap 143.2%  best gap 129.6%
#   T =    6.47  accepted  5.8%  current gap  65.7%  best gap  53.3%
#   T =    3.50  accepted  2.8%  current gap  31.8%  best gap  24.9%
#   T =    1.89  accepted  0.8%  current gap   9.6%  best gap   6.6%
#   T =    1.02  accepted  0.4%  current gap   6.6%  best gap   5.7%
#   T =    0.55  accepted  0.0%  current gap   4.6%  best gap   4.6%
#   T =    0.30  accepted  0.1%  current gap   4.4%  best gap   4.3%
#   T =    0.16  accepted  0.0%  current gap   4.2%  best gap   4.2%
# alpha = 0.80:    54,000 moves per run, mean gap  7.7%, best  3.3%
# alpha = 0.95:   236,000 moves per run, mean gap  3.7%, best  1.4%
# alpha = 0.99: 1,198,000 moves per run, mean gap  2.3%, best  0.3%
```

At $T = 41$, about 60% of moves are accepted and the tour is still almost random. Most of the progress happens between $T \approx 12$ and $T \approx 2$, where the acceptance rate falls from about 20% to 1%. In this range the search can still leave bad configurations but increasingly prefers good ones. Below $T \approx 0.5$ the tour is frozen. Slower cooling gives better tours (mean gaps of 7.7%, 3.7% and 2.3%) at proportionally more moves. Note also that SA with plain 2-opt moves needs over a million moves to reach about 2%, while 2-opt plus Or-opt local search reaches 1-3% from most starts in a fraction of a second. On the TSP, SA is beaten by tailored local search. Its strength is generality.

**Key takeaways**

- SA accepts a worse neighbor with probability $e^{-\Delta/T}$, so it can leave local optima. As $T$ falls it turns into hill climbing.
- At fixed $T$ it samples the Boltzmann distribution. Logarithmic cooling guarantees the optimum in the limit, but practice uses geometric cooling.
- Calibrate $T_0$ from a target acceptance rate. Most progress happens in a middle temperature range, and slower cooling trades time for quality.
- SA is simple and general, but tailored local search usually beats it on well-studied problems.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** An uphill move has $\Delta = 5$. Compute its acceptance probability at $T = 20$, $5$ and $1$. At what temperature is it accepted 10% of the time?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** With a fixed budget of about 240,000 moves, compare $\alpha = 0.95$ with 2,000 moves per temperature, $\alpha = 0.99$ with 400 moves per temperature, and $\alpha = 0.8$ with 9,000 moves per temperature. Which matters more for a fixed budget, the number of temperatures or the moves per temperature?
> 3. **(Interview)** "Evaluating one move in our problem requires a 2-second simulation. Would you choose simulated annealing or tabu search?" *Hint:* count the evaluations per iteration of each method. Then think about surrogate models and parallel evaluation.

#### Tabu Search

**Why it matters.** Tabu search, introduced by Glover in 1986, is one of the most successful metaheuristics for scheduling, vehicle routing, graph coloring and assignment problems. Unlike SA, it is mostly deterministic and makes systematic use of memory. Some of the best known methods for the job shop (the TSAB algorithm of Nowicki and Smutnicki) and for vehicle routing (the unified tabu search of Cordeau, Laporte and Mercier) are tabu searches.

**Theory.** At every iteration, tabu search moves to the **best admissible neighbor**, even if it is worse than the current solution. That lets it walk out of a local optimum. The obvious danger is cycling: from a local optimum, the best move goes uphill, and the best move after that goes straight back down. Tabu search prevents this with memory:

- **Short-term memory (the tabu list).** Recently used *attributes* of moves are forbidden for a number of iterations called the **tenure**. For a 2-opt move that drops the edges $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$, the attribute can be "these edges may not be re-added for $t$ iterations". Storing attributes instead of whole solutions is cheap, but it also forbids some solutions never visited before.
- **Aspiration criterion.** A tabu move is allowed anyway if it produces a new best solution. The tabu rule is a heuristic and must not block a clear improvement.
- **Long-term memory.** Frequency counts of attributes drive **diversification** (penalize moves that were used very often) and **intensification** (restart from elite solutions and explore their common features).
- **Candidate lists.** For large neighborhoods, only a promising subset of moves is evaluated, for example with neighbor lists.

```text
x = best = initial solution
repeat until budget is spent:
    choose the best y in N(x) such that
        the move x -> y is not tabu, OR f(y) < f(best)     # aspiration
    make the attributes of the move tabu for `tenure` iterations
    x = y                                                  # even if f(y) > f(x)
    if f(x) < f(best): best = x
```

The **tenure** is the key parameter. If it is too short, the search cycles. If it is too long, too many moves are forbidden, and the search cannot reach the good regions. Common remedies are random tenures drawn from a range, and **reactive tabu search** (Battiti and Tecchiolli), which increases the tenure when solutions repeat and decreases it otherwise.

**Example: the effect of the tenure.** The code evaluates all 3,000 2-opt moves of the running instance per iteration in one vectorized NumPy computation. A dropped edge becomes tabu for `tenure` iterations, with aspiration. As a cycling detector, it counts the distinct tour lengths visited in the last 500 iterations.

```python
import numpy as np

# Reuses D, n, OPT, length() and nearest_neighbor() from the Nearest Neighbor and Insertion topic.

def tabu_search(t, iters, tenure, seed=0, aspiration=True):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = np.array(t); cur = length(t); best, best_t = cur, t.copy()
    tabu_until = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=int)        # tabu_until[a, b]: edge a-b may not be re-added before
    I, J = np.triu_indices(n, k=2)                  # all 2-opt moves: edges i and j, i < j - 1
    keep = ~((I == 0) & (J == n - 1)); I, J = I[keep], J[keep]
    visited, best_it = [], 0
    for it in range(iters):
        a, b, c, d = t[I], t[I + 1], t[J], t[(J + 1) % n]
        delta = D[a, c] + D[b, d] - D[a, b] - D[c, d]                 # all moves at once
        is_tabu = (tabu_until[a, c] > it) | (tabu_until[b, d] > it)   # would re-add a dropped edge
        allowed = ~is_tabu
        if aspiration:
            allowed |= cur + delta < best - 1e-9    # tabu, but leads to a new best: allow it
        delta = np.where(allowed, delta, np.inf)
        k = np.flatnonzero(delta == delta.min())
        k = k[r.integers(len(k))]                   # best admissible move, even if uphill
        i, j = I[k], J[k]
        for x, y in ((t[i], t[i + 1]), (t[j], t[(j + 1) % n])):       # dropped edges become tabu
            tabu_until[x, y] = tabu_until[y, x] = it + tenure
        t[i + 1:j + 1] = t[i + 1:j + 1][::-1]
        cur += delta[k]
        visited.append(round(cur, 6))
        if cur < best - 1e-9: best, best_t, best_it = cur, t.copy(), it + 1
    return best_t, best_it, visited

start = nearest_neighbor(0)
print(f"start (nearest neighbor): gap {length(start) / OPT - 1:.1%}")
for tenure in (0, 5, 15, 25, 40, 60):
    best_t, best_it, visited = tabu_search(start, iters=3000, tenure=tenure)
    print(f"tenure {tenure:2d}: best gap {length(best_t) / OPT - 1:5.1%} found at iteration {best_it:4d}, "
          f"distinct tour lengths in the last 500 iterations: {len(set(visited[-500:])):3d}")
# start (nearest neighbor): gap 22.7%
# tenure  0: best gap  4.0% found at iteration   16, distinct tour lengths in the last 500 iterations:   2
# tenure  5: best gap  4.0% found at iteration   16, distinct tour lengths in the last 500 iterations:  10
# tenure 15: best gap  2.5% found at iteration   42, distinct tour lengths in the last 500 iterations:  78
# tenure 25: best gap  1.0% found at iteration  927, distinct tour lengths in the last 500 iterations: 500
# tenure 40: best gap  0.8% found at iteration 2642, distinct tour lengths in the last 500 iterations: 500
# tenure 60: best gap  4.0% found at iteration   16, distinct tour lengths in the last 500 iterations: 500
```

With tenure 0, the search reaches a 2-opt local optimum (4.0%) at iteration 16 and then oscillates between two tours forever: the best move goes uphill and the next one undoes it. Tenure 5 produces a longer cycle of 10 tours, and tenure 15 a longer cycle (about 78 distinct tours) that still finds 2.5% on the way. With tenures 25 and 40 the search keeps visiting new tours and reaches 1.0% and 0.8%. Tenure 60 is too restrictive: about 120 recently dropped edges are forbidden at any time. In an 80-city tour, each city's good edges go to its few nearest neighbors, so the search is pushed into poor regions and never improves on its first local optimum.

**Key takeaways**

- Tabu search always moves to the best admissible neighbor, even uphill, and uses short-term memory to avoid cycling.
- Tabu attributes are cheap to store. The aspiration criterion overrides them when a move gives a new best solution.
- The tenure must be long enough to prevent cycling and short enough to keep good moves available. Random or reactive tenures reduce the tuning effort.
- Long-term memory adds intensification and diversification. Candidate lists keep large neighborhoods tractable.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Explain, using the output, why tenure 0 cycles between exactly two tours once it reaches a local optimum.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Give each tabu entry a random tenure drawn uniformly from $[15, 45]$. Compare it with fixed tenures 25 and 40 over 5 different start tours (nearest neighbor from cities 0 to 4).
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you adapt tabu search to a vehicle routing problem with time windows, where most moves are infeasible?" *Hint:* consider accepting infeasible solutions with penalty weights that adapt during the search, attributes such as "customer $i$ in route $r$", and restricting moves to short edges (granular neighborhoods).

#### Genetic Algorithms

**Why it matters.** Genetic algorithms (GAs), introduced by Holland in the 1970s, evolve a **population** of solutions by selection, recombination and mutation, inspired by natural evolution. They need little knowledge of the problem, parallelize naturally, and handle several objectives at once (NSGA-II is the standard method for Pareto fronts, Section 7.1). Their combination with local search, the **memetic algorithm**, is among the best methods known for vehicle routing (the hybrid genetic search of Vidal and coauthors).

**Theory.** A GA needs a **representation** (chromosome) of solutions and five operators:

- **Fitness:** the objective, possibly with penalties for infeasibility.
- **Selection** of parents, biased towards fitness: **tournament** (the best of $k$ random individuals), roulette (probability proportional to fitness) or rank-based.
- **Crossover** (recombination): build a child from two parents, ideally passing on good features of both. For bit strings, use one-point or uniform crossover. For permutations, use special operators that keep the child a valid permutation: **order crossover (OX)**, partially mapped crossover (PMX), and edge recombination or edge assembly crossover (EAX) for the TSP.
- **Mutation:** a small random change (flip a bit, swap or invert a segment) to keep diversity.
- **Replacement:** generational (children replace parents) or steady-state (one child at a time), usually with **elitism** (the best solution always survives).

```text
  Order crossover (OX): keep a slice of parent 1, fill the rest in parent 2's order

  parent 1:  1 2 | 3 4 5 | 6 7 8          slice positions 3-5: 3 4 5
  parent 2:  8 6 | 4 2 7 | 5 3 1          parent 2 read from after the slice: 5 3 1 8 6 4 2 7
                                          skip 3, 4, 5:                       1 8 6 2 7
  child:     2 7 | 3 4 5 | 1 8 6          fill positions 6, 7, 8, then 1, 2
```

**Encodings and constraints.** If a direct representation produces many infeasible children, use a **decoder**: the chromosome is a priority list or a vector of random keys, and a constructive heuristic turns it into a feasible solution. The serial schedule generation scheme for project scheduling (Section 10.2) is the classic decoder: a GA searches over activity lists, and the scheme turns each list into a feasible schedule.

The main risk is **premature convergence**. The population becomes nearly identical before it finds good solutions, and crossover of identical parents produces nothing new. Diversity management (penalizing similar individuals, restarts, islands) is the remedy.

**Example: pure GA versus memetic GA.** The pure GA uses OX, inversion mutation, tournament selection and elitism, with 100 individuals for 500 generations, so 50,000 children. The memetic GA applies 2-opt with neighbor lists to every individual, with 20 individuals for 5 generations.

```python
import numpy as np

# Reuses D, n, OPT and length() from the Nearest Neighbor and Insertion topic,
# and two_opt() from the 2-Opt and k-Opt Moves topic.

def order_crossover(p1, p2, r):
    """OX: copy a random slice of parent 1, fill the rest in parent 2's order."""
    i, j = sorted(r.choice(n, size=2, replace=False))
    child = [None] * n
    child[i:j] = p1[i:j]
    used = set(p1[i:j])
    fill = [c for c in p2[j:] + p2[:j] if c not in used]   # parent 2's order, starting after the slice
    for k, c in zip(list(range(j, n)) + list(range(i)), fill):
        child[k] = c
    return child

def mutate(t, r, rate):
    t = list(t)
    if r.random() < rate:                           # inversion mutation: reverse a random segment
        i, j = sorted(r.choice(n, size=2, replace=False))
        t[i:j] = t[i:j][::-1]
    return t

def genetic_algorithm(pop_size, generations, seed, memetic=False, rate=0.3):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    improve = (lambda t: two_opt(t, neighbor_lists=True)[0]) if memetic else (lambda t: t)
    pop = [improve(list(r.permutation(n))) for _ in range(pop_size)]
    fit = [length(t) for t in pop]
    history = [min(fit) / OPT - 1]                 # generation 0: the initial population
    for g in range(generations):
        def tournament():                           # best of 3 random individuals
            k = r.choice(pop_size, size=3, replace=False)
            return pop[min(k, key=lambda i: fit[i])]
        children = [improve(mutate(order_crossover(tournament(), tournament(), r), r, rate))
                    for _ in range(pop_size)]
        elite = int(np.argmin(fit))                 # elitism: the best individual always survives
        pop = [pop[elite]] + children[:-1]
        fit = [length(t) for t in pop]
        history.append(min(fit) / OPT - 1)
    return min(fit) / OPT - 1, history

_, h = genetic_algorithm(pop_size=100, generations=500, seed=0)
print("pure GA,    100 x 500: best gap at generation 0, 100, ..., 500:",
      " ".join(f"{x:.1%}" for x in h[::100]))
_, h = genetic_algorithm(pop_size=20, generations=5, seed=0, memetic=True)
print("memetic GA,  20 x 5  : best gap at generation 0, 1, ..., 5:    ",
      " ".join(f"{x:.1%}" for x in h))
# pure GA,    100 x 500: best gap at generation 0, 100, ..., 500: 401.3% 172.0% 125.1% 111.8% 99.7% 90.2%
# memetic GA,  20 x 5  : best gap at generation 0, 1, ..., 5:     4.0% 2.8% 0.8% 0.8% 0.8% 0.0%
```

The pure GA improves steadily but slowly. After 50,000 children it is still 90% above the optimum, which is worse than nearest neighbor. OX preserves the relative order of the cities, but in a TSP what matters is which cities are adjacent. Most children inherit few good edges, and blind mutation rarely repairs them. The memetic GA starts from 2-opt local optima (4.0%) and reaches the optimum in the fifth generation, after only 120 local searches. On combinatorial problems, the GA's role is to recombine good local optima, while local search does the fine work. Pure GAs are rarely competitive there.

**Key takeaways**

- A GA evolves a population with selection, crossover, mutation and replacement. Elitism keeps the best solution.
- Crossover must fit the representation. For permutations use OX or PMX, and for the TSP edge-based operators such as EAX.
- Decoders (priority lists, random keys) handle constraints by turning any chromosome into a feasible solution.
- Pure GAs are weak on combinatorial problems. Memetic algorithms (GA plus local search) are among the strongest methods.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Apply OX to parents $(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)$ and $(3, 6, 1, 5, 2, 4)$, keeping positions 2 to 4 of parent 1. Check that the child is a permutation.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Replace OX in the pure GA by an edge-preserving crossover: build the child from the union of the parents' edges, always moving to a neighbor (in either parent) that has the fewest remaining neighbors. How much does the pure GA improve?
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you pick a genetic algorithm over tabu search?" *Hint:* consider objectives that come from a black-box simulator, several objectives at once, cheap parallel evaluation, and whether a natural recombination of two solutions exists.

#### Ant Colony Optimization

**Why it matters.** Ant colony optimization (ACO), introduced by Dorigo in 1992, builds solutions with many simple agents that learn from each other through a shared memory. It works best on problems that are naturally solved by construction, such as routing, sequencing and assignment. Its pheromone memory adapts gradually, which also makes it useful on problems whose data changes over time, such as routing in communication networks.

**Theory.** Real ants lay pheromone as they walk and prefer trails with more pheromone. If two paths lead to food, ants on the shorter path return sooner, so pheromone accumulates faster there and more ants choose it. The colony "finds" the shortest path without any ant knowing it.

ACO for the TSP copies this. Each artificial ant builds a tour city by city. From city $i$ it moves to an unvisited city $j$ with probability

$$
p_{ij} = \frac{\tau_{ij}^{\alpha}\, \eta_{ij}^{\beta}}{\sum_{l \text{ unvisited}} \tau_{il}^{\alpha}\, \eta_{il}^{\beta}},
$$

where $\tau_{ij}$ is the **pheromone** (learned desirability of edge $ij$), $\eta_{ij} = 1 / d_{ij}$ is the **heuristic** information, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ weigh the two. After all ants finish:

- **Evaporation:** $\tau_{ij} \leftarrow (1 - \rho)\, \tau_{ij}$ forgets old information, at rate $\rho$.
- **Deposit:** edges of good tours receive $\Delta\tau = 1 / L$, where $L$ is the tour length.

The main variants differ in who deposits and how:

| Variant | Deposit | Special feature |
|---|---|---|
| Ant System (1992) | every ant | the original version, weak on large instances |
| Ant Colony System | best-so-far ant | greedy choice with probability $q_0$, local pheromone update while building |
| **MAX-MIN Ant System** (Stützle and Hoos, 2000) | iteration-best or best-so-far ant | pheromone kept in $[\tau_{\min}, \tau_{\max}]$ to avoid stagnation, initialized at $\tau_{\max}$ |

The pheromone matrix is a probability model of good solutions that is learned from samples. In this sense ACO belongs to the model-based search methods, together with the cross-entropy method and estimation-of-distribution algorithms. In practice, the best ACO methods apply local search to the ants' tours before depositing.

**Example: MAX-MIN Ant System and the role of $\beta$.** 20 ants per iteration, $\alpha = 1$, $\rho = 0.1$, and no local search.

```python
import numpy as np

# Reuses D, n, OPT, length() and nearest_neighbor() from the Nearest Neighbor and Insertion topic.

def max_min_ant_system(ants, iters, alpha, beta, rho, seed):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    eta = 1.0 / (D + np.eye(n))                     # heuristic desirability: inverse distance
    tau_max = 1.0 / (rho * length(nearest_neighbor(0)))
    tau_min = tau_max / (2 * n)
    tau = np.full((n, n), tau_max)                  # MMAS starts at the upper bound: maximal exploration
    best_t, best_L, log = None, np.inf, []
    for it in range(iters):
        for _ in range(ants):                       # each ant builds a tour city by city
            t = [int(r.integers(n))]
            free = np.ones(n, dtype=bool); free[t[0]] = False
            for _ in range(n - 1):
                w = (tau[t[-1]] ** alpha) * (eta[t[-1]] ** beta) * free  # attractiveness of each free city
                nxt = int(r.choice(n, p=w / w.sum()))
                t.append(nxt); free[nxt] = False
            L = length(t)
            if L < best_L: best_t, best_L = t, L
        tau *= 1 - rho                              # evaporation forgets old information
        for k in range(n):                          # only the best-so-far tour deposits pheromone
            a, b = best_t[k - 1], best_t[k]
            tau[a, b] += 1.0 / best_L; tau[b, a] = tau[a, b]
        tau_max = 1.0 / (rho * best_L)
        np.clip(tau, tau_min, tau_max, out=tau)     # the MAX-MIN bounds prevent stagnation
        if (it + 1) % 25 == 0: log.append(best_L / OPT - 1)
    return best_t, log

for beta in (0, 2, 5):
    _, log = max_min_ant_system(ants=20, iters=150, alpha=1, beta=beta, rho=0.1, seed=0)
    print(f"beta = {beta}: best gap after 25, 50, ..., 150 iterations: "
          + " ".join(f"{g:5.1%}" for g in log))
# beta = 0: best gap after 25, 50, ..., 150 iterations: 368.9% 352.0% 352.0% 352.0% 352.0% 345.0%
# beta = 2: best gap after 25, 50, ..., 150 iterations: 73.2% 13.6%  8.7%  4.7%  3.6%  2.9%
# beta = 5: best gap after 25, 50, ..., 150 iterations: 13.7%  5.7%  3.8%  1.0%  1.0%  1.0%
```

Without heuristic information ($\beta = 0$), ants choose almost at random. The first poor tours deposit pheromone, and the colony reinforces them: after 3,000 tours it is still 345% above the optimum. With $\beta = 2$, the distance guides the construction and the pheromone learns which short edges belong together: 2.9% after 150 iterations. With $\beta = 5$, the colony reaches 1.0% after 100 iterations, using only 2,000 constructed tours. That beats the average SA run with over a million moves. A strong heuristic bias makes the learned pheromone useful much sooner.

**Key takeaways**

- Ants build solutions with probabilities proportional to $\tau^{\alpha} \eta^{\beta}$, combining learned pheromone with greedy heuristic information.
- Evaporation forgets, and deposits on good solutions reinforce. Only the best ants should deposit (MMAS, ACS).
- Pheromone bounds (MMAS) prevent premature stagnation. The heuristic weight $\beta$ is critical.
- ACO is a learned sampling model for constructive problems. Strong implementations add local search.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** An ant at city $i$ can go to three cities with pheromone $\tau = (1, 2, 1)$ and distances $d = (10, 20, 5)$. Compute the transition probabilities for $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 2$, and again for $\beta = 0$.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add 2-opt with neighbor lists (Section 11.1) to the iteration-best tour before the pheromone update. How many iterations does MMAS with $\beta = 2$ then need to reach 1%?
> 3. **(Interview)** "ACO is said to be good for routing packets in networks where traffic changes constantly. Why?" *Hint:* think about evaporation as a forgetting mechanism, about continuous small updates, and about many agents sampling routes in parallel.

#### Particle Swarm Optimization

**Why it matters.** Many optimization problems have continuous variables but an objective that is nonconvex, noisy or available only as a black box: calibrating a simulation model, tuning controller gains, or fitting a model with many local optima. Gradient methods (Chapter 5) find only a local optimum, and the gradient may not even exist. Particle swarm optimization (PSO), proposed by Kennedy and Eberhart in 1995, is a simple population method for these problems, inspired by birds flocking.

**Theory.** A swarm of particles moves through $\mathbb{R}^d$. Particle $i$ has a position $x_i$ (a candidate solution), a velocity $v_i$, and remembers its **personal best** position $p_i$. It also knows the best position $g_i$ found by its **neighborhood** in the swarm. In each iteration:

$$
v_i \leftarrow w\, v_i + c_1 r_1 \odot (p_i - x_i) + c_2 r_2 \odot (g_i - x_i), \qquad x_i \leftarrow x_i + v_i,
$$

where $r_1, r_2$ are vectors of uniform random numbers in $[0, 1]$ and $\odot$ multiplies element by element. The three terms are:

- **inertia** $w\, v_i$: keep moving in the same direction,
- **cognitive** term: return towards your own best memory,
- **social** term: move towards the best point your neighbors found.

The standard **constriction** parameters $w = 0.729$ and $c_1 = c_2 = 1.494$ (Clerc and Kennedy, 2002) keep the swarm stable, so that it converges instead of exploding.

The **topology** decides who counts as a neighbor:

- **Global best (gbest):** every particle follows the best of the whole swarm. Information spreads fast, but the swarm may converge prematurely to one basin.
- **Ring (lbest):** each particle sees only itself and two neighbors. Good positions spread slowly, so several basins are explored in parallel, which makes it more robust on multimodal functions.

PSO handles bounds by clipping and constraints by penalties. Discrete variants exist (binary PSO, random-key encodings for permutations), but PSO is mainly a continuous method.

**Example: the Rastrigin function.** The function

$$
f(x) = 10 d + \sum_{i=1}^{d} \left( x_i^2 - 10 \cos(2 \pi x_i) \right), \qquad x \in [-5.12, 5.12]^d,
$$

has its global minimum $f = 0$ at the origin and a local minimum near every integer point, more than $10^{10}$ of them for $d = 10$. Every method gets 40,000 function evaluations, 10 runs each.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

def rastrigin(X):                                   # global minimum 0 at x = 0, about 10^d local minima
    return 10 * X.shape[-1] + np.sum(X ** 2 - 10 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * X), axis=-1)

DIM, LO, HI, EVALS = 10, -5.12, 5.12, 40_000        # same evaluation budget for every method

def pso(seed, topology, swarm=40, w=0.729, c1=1.49445, c2=1.49445):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = r.uniform(LO, HI, size=(swarm, DIM))        # positions
    V = r.uniform(-1, 1, size=(swarm, DIM))         # velocities
    P, fP = X.copy(), rastrigin(X)                  # personal bests
    for _ in range(EVALS // swarm - 1):
        if topology == "global":                    # every particle follows the swarm's best
            G = np.repeat(P[[fP.argmin()]], swarm, axis=0)
        else:                                       # ring: best of itself and its two neighbors
            idx = np.stack([np.arange(swarm) - 1, np.arange(swarm), (np.arange(swarm) + 1) % swarm])
            G = P[idx[fP[idx].argmin(axis=0), np.arange(swarm)]]
        r1, r2 = r.random((2, swarm, DIM))
        V = w * V + c1 * r1 * (P - X) + c2 * r2 * (G - X)   # inertia + memory + social pull
        X = np.clip(X + V, LO, HI)
        f = rastrigin(X)
        better = f < fP
        P[better], fP[better] = X[better], f[better]
    return fP.min()

def random_search(seed):
    return rastrigin(np.random.default_rng(seed).uniform(LO, HI, size=(EVALS, DIM))).min()

def multistart_lbfgs(seed):
    r, best, used = np.random.default_rng(seed), np.inf, 0
    while used < EVALS:                             # restart from random points until the budget is spent
        res = minimize(lambda x: rastrigin(x), r.uniform(LO, HI, DIM), method="L-BFGS-B",
                       bounds=[(LO, HI)] * DIM)
        used += res.nfev; best = min(best, res.fun)
    return best

for name, method in [("random search", random_search), ("multi-start L-BFGS", multistart_lbfgs),
                     ("PSO, global best", lambda s: pso(s, "global")),
                     ("PSO, ring", lambda s: pso(s, "ring"))]:
    vals = [method(s) for s in range(10)]
    print(f"{name:19s} best f over 10 runs: median {np.median(vals):6.2f}, "
          f"min {min(vals):6.2f}, max {max(vals):6.2f}")
# random search       best f over 10 runs: median  58.93, min  51.06, max  74.04
# multi-start L-BFGS  best f over 10 runs: median  21.39, min  11.94, max  28.85
# PSO, global best    best f over 10 runs: median   8.46, min   3.98, max  13.93
# PSO, ring           best f over 10 runs: median   5.97, min   3.98, max   8.96
```

Random search gets nowhere in 10 dimensions. Multi-start L-BFGS finds a local minimum quickly from each start, but each start lands in a random basin, and estimating gradients by finite differences costs 11 evaluations each. PSO uses the swarm's shared information to concentrate on good regions. The ring topology is better and more consistent (median 5.97, worst 8.96) than the global-best topology, which converges faster but sometimes to a worse basin. A value of 3.98 means 4 coordinates sit near $\pm 1$, a local minimum next to the global one, and no method found the global optimum. On multimodal landscapes, PSO is a good tool for a good solution, not for a certified optimum.

**Key takeaways**

- Each particle combines inertia, attraction to its own best position and attraction to its neighbors' best position.
- Constriction parameters ($w = 0.729$, $c_1 = c_2 = 1.494$) keep the swarm stable. The topology trades speed (gbest) for robustness (ring).
- PSO suits continuous, nonconvex, black-box problems. Use gradient methods for smooth convex problems and LP or MIP solvers for linear models.
- Like all metaheuristics, PSO gives no proof of optimality.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** A particle in 2D is at $x = (1, 2)$ with velocity $v = (0.5, -0.5)$, personal best $p = (0, 2)$ and neighborhood best $g = (2, 0)$. With $w = 0.7$, $c_1 = c_2 = 1.5$, and random numbers $r_1 = (0.2, 0.6)$, $r_2 = (0.5, 0.1)$, compute the new velocity and position.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run the comparison on the Rosenbrock function, which is unimodal but has a narrow curved valley. Which method wins now, and why?
> 3. **(Interview)** "Would you use PSO to solve a linear program with 10,000 variables?" *Hint:* compare what an LP solver guarantees (optimality, duals, speed) with what PSO offers. Then name problems where PSO is the right tool.

#### GRASP

**Why it matters.** The Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), introduced by Feo and Resende, is a disciplined form of multi-start. Every iteration builds a new solution with a randomized greedy heuristic and improves it with local search. It is easy to implement on top of an existing greedy algorithm and local search, its iterations are independent and run in parallel, and it has been applied to hundreds of problems, from set covering to network design.

**Theory.** Each GRASP iteration has two phases, and the best solution over all iterations is returned:

1. **Greedy randomized construction.** At each step, score the candidates with the greedy function, put the best ones in a **restricted candidate list** (RCL), and pick one of them **at random**.
2. **Local search** from the constructed solution.

The RCL can be built in two ways:

- **Cardinality-based:** the $k$ best candidates. $k = 1$ is pure greedy.
- **Value-based:** every candidate with $c \le c_{\min} + \alpha\,(c_{\max} - c_{\min})$. $\alpha = 0$ is pure greedy and $\alpha = 1$ is pure random.

The parameter controls a trade-off. Pure greedy builds good starting points, but always the same ones, so local search always ends in the same local optimum. Pure random gives maximum diversity, but poor starts that need long local searches and often end in worse local optima. Good values are in between, and **reactive GRASP** adapts $\alpha$ by sampling values with probabilities proportional to their past success.

GRASP iterations have no memory of each other. Two standard extensions add some:

- **Path relinking:** walk from one elite solution towards another, one move at a time, and apply local search to the best intermediate solution. Good solutions often share structure, and the path between them explores it.
- **Elite pools and bias functions:** keep the best solutions, and bias the construction towards their features.

**Example: the size of the RCL.** The randomized nearest neighbor always starts at city 0 and picks at random among the $k$ nearest unvisited cities. Each setting runs 30 iterations with 2-opt plus Or-opt.

```python
import numpy as np

# Reuses D, n, OPT and length() from the Nearest Neighbor and Insertion topic,
# and two_opt_or_opt() from the 2-Opt and k-Opt Moves topic.

def randomized_nearest_neighbor(k, r):
    """Greedy randomized construction: pick at random among the k nearest unvisited cities."""
    tour, left = [0], set(range(1, n))
    while left:
        cand = np.array(sorted(left))
        rcl = cand[np.argsort(D[tour[-1], cand])[:k]]   # restricted candidate list
        nxt = int(r.choice(rcl))
        tour.append(nxt); left.remove(nxt)
    return tour

def grasp(k, iters, seed):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    built, improved = [], []
    for _ in range(iters):
        t = randomized_nearest_neighbor(k, r)          # phase 1: greedy randomized construction
        built.append(length(t))
        improved.append(length(two_opt_or_opt(t)))     # phase 2: local search
    return np.array(built), np.array(improved)

print(" RCL size k   construction   after LS (mean)   after LS (best)   local optima   hits of OPT")
for k in (1, 2, 3, 5, 10, n):
    built, improved = grasp(k, iters=30, seed=0)
    print(f"{k:11d} {built.mean() / OPT - 1:14.1%} {improved.mean() / OPT - 1:17.1%} "
          f"{improved.min() / OPT - 1:17.1%} {len(set(np.round(improved, 4))):14d} "
          f"{np.sum(improved < OPT + 1e-3):13d}")
#  RCL size k   construction   after LS (mean)   after LS (best)   local optima   hits of OPT
#           1          22.7%              3.2%              3.2%              1             0
#           2          63.3%              4.2%              0.3%             29             0
#           3         100.3%              3.6%              0.0%             30             1
#           5         149.9%              3.5%              0.0%             28             2
#          10         234.7%              3.6%              0.0%             30             1
#          80         486.5%              4.2%              0.0%             28             1
```

With $k = 1$ the construction is deterministic, so all 30 iterations produce the same local optimum, 3.2% above the optimum: no amount of repetition helps. With $k = 2$, the 30 iterations give 29 different local optima and the best is 0.3%. From $k = 3$ on, GRASP finds the optimum. The construction quality gets much worse with $k$ (486% for a random start), but the average after local search barely moves on this small instance. What the randomization adds is diversity. On larger instances, poor starts cost more local-search time and give worse local optima, which is why small values ($k$ = 2 to 5, or $\alpha$ = 0.1 to 0.3) are common.

**Key takeaways**

- GRASP repeats two phases: a greedy construction randomized by a restricted candidate list, then local search. It keeps the best result.
- The RCL size ($k$ or $\alpha$) trades the quality of starting points against diversity. Pure greedy produces one local optimum only.
- Reactive GRASP adapts $\alpha$. Path relinking and elite pools add memory between iterations.
- Iterations are independent, so GRASP parallelizes almost perfectly.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Five candidates have greedy costs 4, 5, 7, 12 and 20. List the value-based RCL for $\alpha = 0$, $0.25$ and $1$.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add path relinking to the GRASP example: for the two best tours found, apply 2-opt moves that each add an edge of the target tour, evaluate every intermediate tour, and run local search from the best one. Does it find better tours than more GRASP iterations would?
> 3. **(Interview)** "GRASP is embarrassingly parallel. What do we lose by running 1,000 independent iterations on 1,000 cores?" *Hint:* think about what later iterations could learn from earlier ones (reactive $\alpha$, elite pools, path relinking) and how to share it cheaply.

#### Large Neighborhood Search

**Why it matters.** Real routing and scheduling problems come with many side constraints: time windows, driver breaks, vehicle types, precedences. Classic small moves such as 2-opt often turn a feasible solution into an infeasible one, and designing a move for every constraint is impractical. Large Neighborhood Search (LNS), introduced by Shaw in 1998, avoids this. It repeatedly **destroys** part of the solution and **repairs** it, and the repair step handles the constraints. Its adaptive version (ALNS) by Ropke and Pisinger (2006) is one of the most widely used methods for vehicle routing in industry.

**Theory.** Each iteration:

1. **Destroy:** remove $q$ elements (customers, jobs, assignments) from the current solution. The size $q$ is typically 10-40% of the solution.
2. **Repair:** reinsert them with a heuristic (greedy or regret insertion), or with an exact method such as constraint programming or a small MIP.
3. **Accept or reject** the new solution: only if better, with an SA-like rule, or within a threshold of the best.

The neighborhood (all solutions reachable by destroying $q$ elements and repairing them) is exponentially large, but the repair heuristic searches it efficiently. Diversity comes from the choice of destroy operator:

| Destroy operator | Removes | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Random removal | $q$ random customers | diversification |
| Worst removal | customers whose removal saves the most (randomized) | fix badly placed customers |
| Related (Shaw) removal | a seed customer and the customers most similar to it (close in space or time) | let similar customers swap places |
| Route or cluster removal | a whole route or a geographic cluster | reduce the number of vehicles, rebuild regions |

Repair operators are greedy insertion (each customer at its cheapest feasible position) and **regret-$k$ insertion**, which first inserts the customer with the largest difference between its best and $k$-th best insertion cost (the regret idea of the Greedy Heuristics topic).

**Adaptive LNS (ALNS)** keeps a weight $w$ for every operator and chooses operators with probability proportional to their weights. After each iteration, the operators used get a score $\sigma$, for example 10 for a new best solution, 5 for an improvement of the current one and 1 for an accepted one. Their weights are then updated as

$$
w \leftarrow (1 - r)\, w + r\, \sigma,
$$

with a reaction factor $r$ such as 0.1. ALNS thus learns online which operators work on the instance at hand.

**Example: capacitated vehicle routing.** The 80 cities of the running instance become customers with demands from 1 to 9. A depot is at the center, and each vehicle carries 60 units. Each method runs 1,500 iterations with SA-like acceptance, removing 5 to 15 customers per iteration. The starting solution inserts the customers greedily in random order. The `alns()` function can also record every route it produces, a feature the Matheuristics topic uses.

```python
import numpy as np

# Reuses pts from the Nearest Neighbor and Insertion topic: the 80 cities become customers.
r0 = np.random.default_rng(1)
P = np.vstack([[50, 50], pts])                      # node 0 is a central depot
C = np.linalg.norm(P[:, None] - P[None, :], axis=2)
q = np.concatenate([[0], r0.integers(1, 10, size=80)])   # demands
Q = 60                                              # vehicle capacity

def cost(routes):
    return sum(C[0, r[0]] + sum(C[a, b] for a, b in zip(r, r[1:])) + C[r[-1], 0] for r in routes if r)

def insertion_options(routes, c):
    """(extra cost, route index, position) of every feasible place for customer c."""
    opts = [(C[0, c] * 2, len(routes), 0)]          # a new route of its own
    for k, r in enumerate(routes):
        if sum(q[r]) + q[c] > Q: continue
        path = [0] + r + [0]
        for p in range(len(path) - 1):
            opts.append((C[path[p], c] + C[c, path[p + 1]] - C[path[p], path[p + 1]], k, p))
    return sorted(opts)

def place(routes, c, k, p):
    if k == len(routes): routes.append([c])
    else: routes[k].insert(p, c)

# ---- destroy operators: remove `m` customers, return the partial solution and the removed list
def random_removal(routes, m, r):
    out = set(r.choice(np.arange(1, 81), size=m, replace=False))
    return [[c for c in rt if c not in out] for rt in routes], list(out)

def worst_removal(routes, m, r):
    saving = {}                                     # how much each customer costs where it is
    for rt in routes:
        path = [0] + rt + [0]
        for i in range(1, len(path) - 1):
            saving[path[i]] = C[path[i - 1], path[i]] + C[path[i], path[i + 1]] - C[path[i - 1], path[i + 1]]
    ranked = sorted(saving, key=lambda c: -saving[c])
    out = set()
    while len(out) < m:                             # randomized: favor, but do not force, the worst
        out.add(ranked[int(len(ranked) * r.random() ** 4)])
    return [[c for c in rt if c not in out] for rt in routes], list(out)

def related_removal(routes, m, r):
    seed = int(r.integers(1, 81))                   # a customer and its nearest customers
    near = [c for c in np.argsort(C[seed]) if c != 0][:m]
    out = set(near)
    return [[c for c in rt if c not in out] for rt in routes], list(out)

# ---- repair operators
def greedy_repair(routes, removed, r):
    for c in r.permutation(removed):                # each customer at its cheapest feasible place
        _, k, p = insertion_options(routes, c)[0]
        place(routes, c, k, p)
    return [rt for rt in routes if rt]

def regret_repair(routes, removed, r):
    removed = list(removed)
    while removed:                                  # insert first the customer with most to lose
        best = None
        for c in removed:
            o = insertion_options(routes, c)
            regret = o[1][0] - o[0][0] if len(o) > 1 else np.inf
            if best is None or regret > best[0]: best = (regret, c, o[0])
        _, c, (_, k, p) = best
        place(routes, c, k, p); removed.remove(c)
    return [rt for rt in routes if rt]

def alns(destroys, repairs, iters, seed, adaptive, pool=None):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    cur = greedy_repair([], list(range(1, 81)), r)  # initial solution: insert everyone greedily
    best, start = cur, cost(cur)
    w_d, w_r = np.ones(len(destroys)), np.ones(len(repairs))
    T = 0.02 * start                                # SA-style acceptance, cooled linearly
    for it in range(iters):
        i = r.choice(len(destroys), p=w_d / w_d.sum()) if adaptive else r.integers(len(destroys))
        j = r.choice(len(repairs), p=w_r / w_r.sum()) if adaptive else r.integers(len(repairs))
        m = int(r.integers(5, 16))                  # remove 5-15 customers
        partial, removed = destroys[i]([list(rt) for rt in cur], m, r)
        cand = repairs[j](partial, removed, r)
        if pool is not None:                        # remember every route seen (Matheuristics topic)
            for rt in cand:
                key = frozenset(rt)
                if key not in pool or cost([rt]) < cost([pool[key]]): pool[key] = rt
        temp = T * (1 - it / iters)
        score = 0
        if cost(cand) < cost(best) - 1e-9: best, score = cand, 10      # new best solution
        if cost(cand) < cost(cur) - 1e-9: score = max(score, 5)       # improves the current one
        if cost(cand) < cost(cur) - 1e-9 or r.random() < np.exp(-(cost(cand) - cost(cur)) / max(temp, 1e-9)):
            cur, score = cand, max(score, 1)
        if adaptive:                                # reward operators that produced good solutions
            w_d[i] = 0.9 * w_d[i] + 0.1 * score
            w_r[j] = 0.9 * w_r[j] + 0.1 * score
            w_d, w_r = np.maximum(w_d, 0.1), np.maximum(w_r, 0.1)
    return start, best, w_d / w_d.sum(), w_r / w_r.sum()

print(f"total demand {q.sum()}, capacity {Q}: at least {int(np.ceil(q.sum() / Q))} vehicles")
for name, D_ops, R_ops, adaptive in [
        ("LNS (random removal, greedy repair)", [random_removal], [greedy_repair], False),
        ("ALNS (3 destroy x 2 repair, adaptive)", [random_removal, worst_removal, related_removal],
         [greedy_repair, regret_repair], True)]:
    for seed in range(2):
        start, best, wd, wr = alns(D_ops, R_ops, iters=1500, seed=seed, adaptive=adaptive)
        print(f"{name} seed {seed}: initial {start:6.1f} -> best {cost(best):6.1f} "
              f"with {len(best)} routes" + (f"   destroy weights {np.round(wd, 2)}, repair {np.round(wr, 2)}"
                                            if adaptive else ""))
# total demand 392, capacity 60: at least 7 vehicles
# LNS (random removal, greedy repair) seed 0: initial 2178.8 -> best  979.0 with 7 routes
# LNS (random removal, greedy repair) seed 1: initial 2038.9 -> best  966.9 with 7 routes
# ALNS (3 destroy x 2 repair, adaptive) seed 0: initial 2178.8 -> best  964.4 with 7 routes   destroy weights [0.43 0.4  0.18], repair [0.42 0.58]
# ALNS (3 destroy x 2 repair, adaptive) seed 1: initial 2038.9 -> best  954.6 with 7 routes   destroy weights [0.42 0.41 0.17], repair [0.53 0.47]
```

Both methods turn a poor starting solution (over 2,000) into routes of about 955-980 with 7 vehicles, the minimum the total demand allows. ALNS with three destroy and two repair operators beats plain LNS on both seeds. Its learned weights are informative: random and worst removal get about 40% each, while related removal gets less than 20% on this instance. A different instance, for example with time windows, could produce quite different weights. That is exactly why the weights are learned rather than fixed.

**Key takeaways**

- LNS alternates destroy and repair. Each step explores an exponentially large neighborhood with a heuristic or exact repair method.
- Destroy operators (random, worst, related, route) give diversity. Repair operators (greedy, regret, exact) handle the side constraints.
- ALNS chooses operators adaptively, with weights updated from their recent success.
- LNS is the standard approach for rich vehicle routing and scheduling problems with many constraints.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Customer $c$ sits between $a$ and $b$ with $d(a, c) = 4$, $d(c, b) = 5$ and $d(a, b) = 6$. Compute its removal saving. Another customer has insertion costs 3, 4 and 9 in three routes, and a third has 2, 8 and 9. Which one does regret-2 insert first?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add a **route removal** destroy operator (remove all customers of a random route) and set the capacity to 70. Does ALNS find solutions with 6 vehicles, and which operators gain weight?
> 3. **(Interview)** "Our dispatchers add constraints every month (new vehicle types, driver breaks, customer time windows). Which solution method keeps up best?" *Hint:* compare how much code changes in a local search with specialized moves, in an LNS whose repair step checks feasibility, and in a MIP or CP model.
